title: Connected but Unequal: Cardiovascular Risk Burden and Digital Health Engagement Among US Adults
content: Adults with multiple cardiovascular risk factors may have greater need for digital tools that support prevention of chronic diseases; however, the use and patterns of engagement remain unclear. Using data from the nationally representative Health Information National Trends Survey cycles (2019, 2020, 2022, and 2024) we examined associations between cardiovascular risk-factor burden and digital health engagement among US adults. Five cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, smoking, physical inactivity, and overweight or obesity) were summed and classified as low (0–1), moderate (2–3), or high (4–5) burden. Digital health engagement included online health information seeking, provider messaging, test-result access, appointment scheduling, and wearable-device use (score, 0–5). Multivariable regression models were used to examine associations between cardiovascular risk-factor burden and digital health engagement. Among 16,861 adults, weighted mean (SE) age was 47.2 (0.18) years; 49.5% were male and 63.6% were non-Hispanic White. Risk-factor burden was low in 38.8%, moderate in 51.4%, and high in 9.9%. Adjusted mean engagement scores differed by burden (low, 2.81; moderate, 2.92; high, 2.96; P = .03). Compared with low burden, moderate burden was associated with higher odds of provider messaging (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 1.20; 95% CI, 1.07–1.35) and online test-result access (AOR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.11–1.53). High burden was associated with test-result access (AOR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.21–1.85) and wearable use (AOR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.16–1.78). Greater cardiovascular risk-factor burden was associated with modestly higher digital health engagement, particularly for test-result access, provider messaging, and wearable use.
